But if the virtue of a greater natural heat approaches this quicksilver before it is fashioned to its end, that is to say, into the form of silver, so that it is reduced into the pure and red sulfur of nature, then gold is made from it more quickly than silver, and it remains in that state permanently, which is the end toward which nature strives by working.

Quicksilver, which we just mentioned, is the mother of all metals because of its coldness and humidity; and if it becomes pure and separated from every superfluity, then no further coarseness can be mixed with it, so that it might be reduced back into some imperfect metal. For nature does not work backward, nor is there matter that looks toward an impure form, such as imperfect metals are. But sulfur is the father of all metals because of its heat and dryness. According to this distinction, it should be observed that quicksilver is described in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER II.

There is, therefore, in all metals true Mercury and right sulfur, equally in imperfect as in perfect metals; it is only contaminated and made impure in the imperfect metals, which are the only ones deprived of perfect maturation. And for the same causes, they can be reduced to gold and silver, that is, so that the impurity with which they had been polluted may be separated from the golden or silver nature that is in them, and the form of gold or silver may be instilled into them. For they have been torn away from nature because they have been removed and excavated from natural passages, mines, and veins of the earth; therefore, they can have no further operation in themselves, as if they still lay hidden under the earth; nevertheless, however much is in them, they desire to be perfected.
